# 20/09/2026 12:00 — Plus vs Pro for Product Reviews

**Yes, partner — for the kind of work you are doing, Pro can improve the review quality.** But there is an important distinction: upgrading does **not automatically make every review better**. You need to actually select the higher reasoning level/model.

For your RevRescue review and the other marketplace products, the difference is relevant because you're asking me to simultaneously inspect **ZIP codebases + Excel trackers + architecture + tests + security + market demand + enterprise gaps + sprint planning**.

| Capability | Your current Plus | Pro |
|---|---|---|
| GPT-5.6 Sol | ✅ | ✅ |
| Medium reasoning | ✅ | ✅ |
| High reasoning | ✅ | ✅ |
| **Extra High reasoning** | ❌ | **✅** |
| **GPT-5.6 Sol Pro** | ❌ | **✅** |
| **GPT-6 Pro** | ❌ | **✅** |
| Best suited to very difficult/long-running review | Good | **Better** |

This is the current OpenAI plan distinction. citeturn0search0turn0search2

### For *your* 8-product review project

I would expect the biggest improvement in exactly these areas:

**1. Deeper code reasoning.** Following interactions across many modules, finding architectural contradictions, checking whether tests really exercise production paths, spotting tenancy/security issues, and distinguishing genuine implementation from impressive-looking documentation.

**2. Better cross-file reconciliation.** For example:

> Claude tracker says capability X is complete → source code implements X → tests cover X → architecture document promises X → manual test verifies X.

That's considerably harder than simply reviewing each file separately.

**3. Better enterprise-grade assessment.** Your question isn't merely *"does this code work?"* You're asking whether something can become a commercially credible Salesforce/Stripe/Atlassian/Shopify marketplace product. That requires reasoning across architecture, security, reliability, UX, operations, commercial positioning and competitors.

**4. Better sprint design.** Instead of generating generic "add monitoring / add security / add SSO" recommendations, higher reasoning gives us more room to derive sprints from actual deficiencies and dependencies in the repository.

### But Pro will NOT solve everything

This is important.

Pro does **not** magically turn unexecuted evidence into executed evidence. For example, in RevRescue, Claude says the system has **353 automated tests**, but I wasn't able to independently complete that entire execution during this review. Likewise, the supplied product documentation itself says the product has only reached the **integration** evidence level, not Stripe contract/live/operational proof. fileciteturn0file0L207-L232

No model tier can legitimately convert that into:

> "Enterprise ready — verified."

We still need to execute the tests, inspect the evidence, connect to Stripe test mode, run manual tests, etc.

### One change since you previously used Pro

OpenAI changed this recently. On **14 September 2026**, automatic switching from Instant to Thinking was retired for Plus and Pro. So simply buying Pro and leaving the conversation on **Instant** won't necessarily give your repository review maximum reasoning. citeturn0search4

For these product reviews, I would use:

**Pro + GPT-5.6 Sol + Extra High**, or **GPT-5.6 Sol Pro** for the hardest review passes.

OpenAI describes Sol Pro as the higher-capability option for difficult and longer-running workflows. citeturn0search0

## What I'd do in your position

For ordinary questions, recipes, emails, research, etc., **Plus is already plenty**.

For this specific project—reviewing the **8 marketplace products deeply before Claude continues spending substantial build time**—**Pro has meaningful value**.

But I would not redo everything merely because you upgrade. A better workflow is:

**Claude builds → ChatGPT Pro/Extra High performs adversarial review → Claude fixes → ChatGPT verifies → only then move to the next sprint.**

And for the final portfolio decision, I'd do **one cross-product review of all 8 products together**, because the question isn't just whether each product is technically good. It's also whether we're accidentally building eight technically strong products where only two or three have compelling commercial differentiation.

That final cross-product comparison is where the additional reasoning capability would probably be most valuable for your project. memcite

# 20/09/2026 12:01 — Has the Pro problem been fixed?

Partner, **I would NOT tell you “yes, it is fixed.”** I checked the current information specifically because you had a bad experience after upgrading before.

You remember correctly: in August, after you moved from Plus to Pro, your large ZIP reviews started giving you problems — stalled reviews, files apparently becoming inaccessible, incomplete batches, and repeated attempts where we couldn't continue the review properly. memcite

### What I can verify now

There **have been genuine recent ChatGPT reliability incidents**. OpenAI's status history shows increased error rates for **Pro and Plus conversations on 9 September**, ChatGPT Work errors on 10 September, and GPT-5.6/European ChatGPT errors on 11 September. Those incidents are marked recovered. citeturn0search5turn0search10

There was also a specific **file-upload processing incident on 8 September** where uploaded files could appear uploaded but remain unavailable. OpenAI marks that incident resolved. citeturn0search1

However—and this is the part I don't want to hide from you—there are **very recent user reports from Pro users of GPT-5.6 High/Extra High having trouble with exactly the kind of workload you do**: large files, long analysis, multi-source reconciliation and long-running technical tasks. One report dated **16 September 2026** describes long complex tasks freezing after roughly 25–30 minutes. That's a community report, not an official OpenAI confirmation of a system-wide defect, so I can't say it will happen to you. citeturn0search3

### So should you upgrade today?

For **answer quality**, Pro gives you something useful: Extra High reasoning and GPT-5.6 Sol Pro, which OpenAI explicitly positions for difficult and longer-running workflows. citeturn0search0

For **reliability of huge ZIP reviews**, I **cannot promise Pro will be more reliable than Plus**.

And because *that* was the thing that caused you trouble last time, **I would not upgrade solely because I told you the RevRescue review would become better.**

Notice what just happened on **Plus**: you gave me RevRescue's ZIPs and spreadsheets; I inspected the code/documents, researched the market, found engineering issues, built the S22–S35 roadmap, and successfully produced your Excel review.

**That workflow is currently working.**

My suggestion is therefore: **continue the 8-product reviews on Plus for now.** Once all eight are reviewed, if we want one exceptionally deep **cross-product portfolio review**, that's where trying Pro/Extra High could have real value. But I wouldn't risk disrupting the currently working workflow just for the expectation that every individual review will suddenly become much better.

So the answer to **“has the problem that hurt me last time definitely been fixed?” is: no, I don't have evidence strong enough to tell you that.**

# 20/09/2026 11:58 — RevRescue Stripe Review V001

Partner, I completed the review across the **v017 codebase, v021 tracker, product diagram, version/manual-test workbook**, plus current market evidence for Stripe recovery competitors.

**Review workbook:**  
[Download chatgpt_review_V001-revrescue_stripe_20260920_1158.xlsx](sandbox:/mnt/data/chatgpt_review_V001-revrescue_stripe_20260920_1158.xlsx)

### Main conclusions

**Market demand: YES — the category is proven.** Stripe itself provides Smart Retries, card updater and failed-payment recovery, while dedicated products such as Churnkey and Baremetrics charge specifically for payment recovery/dunning. citeturn0search9turn0search2turn0search0 This means RevRescue is addressing a genuine commercial problem, but also entering a **competitive market where basic retry + email functionality is not enough**.

**Enterprise-grade today: NO.** It is currently a **strong pre-production/integration-tested backend**, not an enterprise production product. Claude's own product status confirms that nothing has yet communicated with Stripe, contract/live/operational evidence has not been reached, the merchant UI is absent, production infrastructure is not established, and external penetration/developer review remains outstanding. fileciteturn0file0L59-L62 fileciteturn0file0L207-L232

There is nevertheless substantial engineering underneath it: tenant RLS, immutable statements, recovery attribution, reversals/credits, audit chaining, DLQ/operator functions, privacy operations and fail-closed configuration. The supplied diagram describes these as built and integration-tested. fileciteturn0file0L235-L239

One important enterprise security issue I identified from the repository documentation is that the application database login can switch between tenant and system roles. The project's own `OPERATIONS.md` acknowledges that SQL injection could therefore escalate to system scope. My roadmap specifically requires **separate database identities/credentials and removal of that escalation path**, rather than relying only on parameterised SQL.

### What Claude should build next

I created **14 enhancement sprints, S22–S35**, rather than simply adding more internal unit functionality:

**S22–S24** establish real Stripe contracts, the complete recovery loop, and production messaging. **S25–S26** build the merchant experience and settle pricing/causal attribution. **S27–S30** establish production infrastructure, stronger isolation/security, enterprise identity and SRE/observability. **S31–S32** address compliance and independent security assurance. **S33** is especially important: 5–10 real design partners and measurement of incremental recovery versus their existing Stripe baseline. **S34–S35** then add adaptive recovery intelligence and Marketplace launch readiness.

That ordering matters because Stripe already claims its own automated tools recover failed payments and provides Smart Retries and card updating. citeturn0search8turn0search9 Churnkey also offers segmentation, A/B testing, retry logic, integrations and enterprise features, while Baremetrics combines dunning with branded payment-update experiences and SMS/email outreach. citeturn0search2turn0search1 RevRescue therefore needs to demonstrate **incremental recovery and superior operational evidence**, not merely feature parity.

The uploaded status document itself identifies **DEC-04/D14 as the immediate blocker**: Stripe connectors/test account must be unparked before the contract and live evidence can be produced. fileciteturn0file0L244-L250

### Workbook contents

The review contains **Executive Review, Market Demand, Enterprise Gap, Sprint Roadmap, Code Findings, Release Gates, and Evidence Sources**. I also recorded an important verification limitation: I attempted to independently execute the automated suite; the initial run could not compile because dependencies had not yet been installed, and the subsequent `npm ci` + test execution exceeded the available execution window. Therefore I **did not falsely certify Claude's claimed 353 passing tests**. The supplied manual-test workbook also has all **56 manual cases still awaiting execution**.

The key direction is: **do not abandon RevRescue**. The problem has market demand and the backend foundation is substantial. But the next investment should go into **real Stripe integration → real merchant UX → real production operation → external security → real customer/ROI evidence**, rather than another long sequence of isolated internal hardening.

Context — what you are looking at

RevRescue recovers failed subscription payments for Stripe merchants. When a payment fails it retries at a sensible moment, reminds the customer over four days, offers a deal to anyone cancelling, records which of those actions recovered the money, and bills the merchant a share of what it recovered.

The diagram below is the whole product on one page. Colour shows how far each part has been built. The important thing to understand before reading it: nothing in RevRescue has ever talked to Stripe. That is not an oversight — it is decision D14, which parks the Stripe connectors until you take it. Everything that could be built without Stripe has been built and tested.

What is complete

CapabilityStatusWhat that means in practice
Recovering a failed payment: retry timing, reminders, save offersBuiltEvery rule is tested; the scheduler drains its own queue and cannot send a reminder twice.
Knowing which payment we recovered, and proving itBuiltAttribution records the evidence; the merchant can read it, and a payment we did not act on is never billed.
Charging the merchant: monthly statement, cap, trial, creditsBuiltPer month and per currency, immutable once issued, with credits that converge exactly. Checked on 400 random histories and by mutation testing at 99.1%.
Not charging a customer twiceBuiltEvery attempt has a stable key stored before the call; after a crash the invoice state is read first.
Keeping merchants apartBuiltThe database itself filters by tenant on all 20 account tables; crafted cross-tenant reads and writes are refused.
Proving nothing was alteredBuiltEach audit row is chained to the previous one; the merchant can verify their own trail, and edits are detected.
Not losing workBuiltRepeated failures park the work with a dead letter that an authenticated operator can replay or discard.
Privacy promises: export, delete, opt-out, retentionBuiltDelete covers every table holding account data, opt-outs survive restarts and stop both channels, retention runs on a schedule.
Access control: roles, revocation, team changesBuiltRemoving or demoting someone ends their session at once; the last owner cannot be removed.
Safety net around the build itselfBuiltSeven checks fail the build, including money rules and a check that published promises have code behind them.

# 20/09/2026 12:04 — Don't Upgrade Just for One Test

Yes, partner — **that's the problem with my previous suggestion.** Doing *“one review on Pro and compare it with Plus”* isn't a sensible experiment if upgrading commits your account to Pro for the billing period.

OpenAI's current billing information says an **upgrade takes effect immediately and starts a new billing cycle**, while moving to a lower tier takes effect at the **next renewal**. So you can't simply test Pro for a day and immediately return to Plus. citeturn0search5

There's another important change **right now**: OpenAI says that since **10 September 2026**, new upgrades to the **$200 Pro (20x)** tier are temporarily paused. The **$100 Pro tier remains available**, with about **5× Plus usage**, while the $200 tier is 20× Plus. citeturn0search5

So I would change my earlier recommendation:

**Stay on Plus for these eight product reviews.**

We already know the current Plus workflow can handle RevRescue: ZIP + multiple Excel files + code review + market research + enterprise assessment + sprint roadmap + generated review workbook.

More importantly, your previous experience matters. You upgraded before specifically expecting these large reviews to improve, and instead you experienced stalled/failed ZIP review workflows. I cannot guarantee that won't happen again. memcite

Let's finish **all 8 products on Plus first** using the same review standard. Then we can create the portfolio-level comparison on Plus too. If at some later point there is a compelling reason for Pro—not merely *“maybe the answer will be a little better”*—we can reconsider it.

**I wouldn't spend the money or lock yourself into a Pro billing cycle just to run my proposed A/B test.**
